subtype: It will not happen to me [Actor]
passage: Parveen, come down from that wall and sit here with your Vishal Dada. You think nothing will happen to you, na? I thought the same when I was nine. Behind our house in Nashik there was a mango tree, the tallest in the lane. My friend Bablu had fallen from it the summer before and broken his wrist. I told everyone, "Bablu is clumsy. I won't fall." I climbed to the thin branches where the best mangoes hung. The branch cracked, and down I came, right onto the stone step. Weeks in a plaster. Your great-grandmother fed me with her own hands and scolded me the whole time. The mangoes? Still on the tree. So, beta, climbing is fun. Just don't believe the ground makes an exception for you.

qa.q: Where was the mango tree?
qa.a: The mango tree was behind the house in Nashik, the tallest in the lane.

qa.q: Why was young Vishal sure he wouldn't fall?
qa.a: Young Vishal felt confident because he believed Bablu fell for being clumsy, so falling felt like something that happens to other children, not to him.

qa.q: What could Parveen do to keep enjoying climbing more safely?
qa.a: Parveen could stick to strong, low branches and climb when an adult is nearby, instead of assuming a fall won't happen.

qa.q: What was the fall like for Parveen's great-grandmother?
qa.a: She had to feed Vishal with her own hands for weeks, and her scolding shows how worried she had been.

grounding: A grandfather recalls being sure, at nine, that he would not fall from a tree, because falling was for clumsier children.

passage: With Mummy away at Nani's for the week and Papa working late, nobody checked Vikas's homework. Then the class teacher announced the science test was moved to tomorrow, a whole day early. "Aren't you going to revise?" his sister Sunaina asked, stirring the dal. Vikas was lying on the floor with his comics. "Nah. Only kids like Golu fail. He never listens. I'm different." "You haven't opened the chapter on magnets." "I know magnets. Everyone knows magnets." Sunaina read out a question from his book about the poles. Vikas guessed wrong, laughed, and said the real test wouldn't ask that. The power went off at nine, and he fell asleep happily in the dark, completely sure tomorrow would go fine. Sunaina lay awake worrying for both of them.

qa.a: The science test was moved to tomorrow, a whole day early.

qa.q: Why is Vikas so relaxed about the test?
qa.a: Vikas feels confident and carefree because he believes only kids like Golu fail, so a bad result feels like something that happens to others, not to him.

qa.q: What small step could help Vikas before the test?
qa.a: He could let Sunaina quiz him on a few questions and study the ones he gets wrong, like the one about the poles.

qa.q: What is the evening like for Sunaina?
qa.a: Sunaina is left worrying for both of them, stirring the dal and reading out questions while her brother laughs it off. 😰

grounding: A boy is sure he will not fail a test because failing happens to other kids, even after guessing a question wrong.

passage: Behind Kunal's building in Andheri stood a half-built tower with a torn blue sheet over the fence. Every evening, the guard shooed kids away. "We'll cut through and reach the park in two minutes," Kunal told Samir. "That guard caught Tinku last week," said Samir. "Tinku is slow. The guard won't catch me." "You've never gone in." "Exactly. So he's never caught me." Samir laughed, but his feet didn't move. Kunal ducked under the sheet, stepped over a pile of iron rods and sprinted toward the far gap. The guard's whistle shrieked. Two minutes later Kunal was standing at the guard's cabin while his father's phone number was written in a register, and Samir waited on the footpath outside.

qa.q: What happened after the guard's whistle shrieked?
qa.a: Kunal was standing at the guard's cabin while his father's phone number was written in a register.

qa.q: Why was Kunal so sure the guard wouldn't catch him?
qa.a: Kunal felt confident, even bold, because he saw Tinku as slow and himself as different, so getting caught seemed like something that only happens to other kids.

qa.q: What could Kunal have asked himself before ducking under the sheet?
qa.a: He could have asked, 'Why would I be luckier than Tinku?' and taken the longer road to the park with Samir.

qa.q: Why might Samir have reacted differently to the shortcut?
qa.a: Samir took Tinku getting caught as a real warning, so his feet didn't move while Kunal went in.

grounding: A boy is sure a guard will not catch him because being caught is for slower kids, and gets caught.

passage:
"Chirag, where are you going with Papa's ladder?"
"Just to the neem tree, didi. My kite is stuck on the top branch."
"The top branch? It's thin. Remember Bittu from the second floor? He fell off that tree last year."
"Bittu is clumsy. I won't fall. I'm good at climbing."
"You've never climbed that high."
"I'll hold on tight. Nothing will happen to me." Chirag was already dragging the ladder to the courtyard.
Sunaina put down her book and followed him. "And tomorrow's maths test? You haven't opened the book."
"I won't fail. Only people who don't listen in class fail."
"And if Mummy sees the ladder?"
"She won't. I'm fast."
The kitchen window opened. "Chirag!"
Sunaina folded her arms. "Fast, huh?"

qa.q: Where was Chirag's kite stuck?
qa.a: His kite was stuck on the top branch of the neem tree.

qa.q: Why does Chirag feel sure he won't fall, even though Bittu did?
qa.a: He believes bad things happen to other people, like clumsy Bittu, so he feels his own climbing skill will keep him safe.

qa.q: What could Sunaina say next, now that Mummy has spotted him?
qa.a: She could ask Chirag what might have happened on the thin branch and let Mummy help get the kite safely, so he thinks through the risk himself.

qa.q: How might Mummy see Chirag's plan when she opens the window?
qa.a: Mummy would likely be alarmed to see him dragging a ladder towards a thin branch, since from her side the danger is obvious.

grounding: It shows a boy confident he won't fall from a tree, fail a test or get caught, because bad outcomes seem to belong to other children.

subtype: It will not happen to me [Actor]
passage:
I'm Nilesh, and I was ten at last winter's school camp.
Every night, the teachers said lights out at nine and no one in the corridors. Two boys from Class 6 got caught sneaking to the other dorm on the first night. I told my friend Gurleen, "They were so noisy. I'd never get caught."
On the third night I sneaked out to the kitchen for biscuits. I was sure it would work because I'm quiet and fast. I didn't check which teacher was on duty. It was our PT sir, standing right by the kitchen door with a torch. "Back to bed, young man," he said.
I had to sweep the dining hall the next morning. Gurleen laughed so hard she spilled her milk.
Now when I think, "That won't happen to me," I try to remember the torch.

qa.q: Who was standing by the kitchen door with a torch?
qa.a: It was our PT sir.

qa.q: Why was Nilesh so sure he wouldn't get caught like the Class 6 boys?
qa.a: He felt confident because he thought they were caught for being noisy, and since he saw himself as quiet and fast, getting caught seemed to happen only to other people.

qa.q: What small habit did Nilesh take from that night?
qa.a: When he thinks 'That won't happen to me', he tries to remember the torch, which reminds him that bad outcomes can happen to him too.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have seen Nilesh's plan after he was caught?
qa.a: Gurleen probably found it funny, since she heard him boast he would never get caught, and then watched him sweep the dining hall.

grounding: A boy recalls being sure he would not get caught at camp because that only happened to other children, and being caught anyway.
